title: thermal storage heats up industry hunts cheaper cleaner energy  ecmii 2026 04 21
text:
April 21 - From the glass screen and metal components in your mobile phone to the plastic shampoo bottle you reach for in your morning shower, our daily lives depend on materials that have been produced and manufactured using heat.
Across the globe, 37% of total energy is used by industry, and two-thirds of industrial energy consumption is in the form of heat. But industry has proven stubbornly difficult to decarbonise, with fossil fuels, mainly natural gas, still powering about 80%.
While the dramatic drop in renewable energy prices has made electrification a more commercially viable alternative, ​industrial processes require process heat 24/7, meaning some form of energy storage is needed to cope with the intermittency of renewables.
Battery energy storage is one solution, (cross-ref to mining story), but there’s another form of storage that is gaining ground: ‌thermal energy storage. In TES, energy is stored directly in a medium, like water, molten salt, sand, rock or concrete, generally through a change of temperature, and released when it is needed, days or even months later. Waste heat from one high-temperature industrial process can be stored and used for another purpose, such as space heating or hot water.
Antoine Koen, an analyst at nonprofit think-tank Future Cleantech Architects, based in Germany, say TES can be as much as five times cheaper than lithium-ion battery storage systems, as the materials used to manufacture them are readily available.
“These technologies – we’re talking steel tanks, steel pipes, very abundant materials like gravel, carbon, molten salts – there’s really ​zero bottleneck in terms of material availability,” says Koen. European and American companies are also very comfortable with the industrial engineering side of things, he adds: “They've been doing this for 200 years”.
Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the Environmental ​Change Institute, University of Oxford, says five years ago there were only a handful of pilot projects. Today the thermal energy storage industry is valued at $2.51 billion, with dozens of companies developing and offering solutions ⁠across multiple use cases.
While hydrogen is often presented as the default solution for industrial heat, Rosenow says that in reality there are several competing options. Direct electrification (ie electric arc furnaces, electric boilers, resistive or induction heating) is possible, but “thermal storage can be particularly powerful in industrial contexts,” ​he explains. “By storing heat when electricity is abundant and cheap, facilities can decouple heat production from real-time electricity supply. This reduces peak demand, lowers costs and eases pressure on the power system.”
Morten Bülow is the CEO of Norway-based Kyoto Group, which has developed a “Heatcube” TES system. Heatcube uses molten ​salt as the thermal medium and provides customers with steam at 150-300 degrees Celsius. Bülow says Kyoto works with potential customers to analyse whether this system makes sense for them, depending on the availability of cheap electricity in their location, how much steam is required and at what temperature.
Customers can either choose heat-as-a-service, purchasing green steam without upfront investment, operational risk or maintenance costs, or heat-as-a-product, where they own and operate the system.
In October Kyoto Group inaugurated its second European Heatcube at KALL Ingredients’ corn-processing facility in Hungary, under a heat as a service agreement. “We take all the risk, so our customer only ​pays for the heat that they're actually using,” says Bülow.
The 56 megawatt hours (MWh) Heatcube will replace natural gas, providing more than 20 gigawatt hours (GWh) of clean process heat annually over the 15-year agreement, reducing more than 8,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions.
“One of our big tasks is to help ​people understand that [TES] gives them an option to decarbonise, but the honest truth is that decarbonisation is not necessarily as high on the agenda as it was five years ago,” says Bülow. These days, he says, they are leading more with the cost savings aspect.
He could not divulge exactly how much KALL, ‌for example, will ⁠save, but says that in most cases across Europe, they see “a substantial reduction in energy costs when replacing gas boilers with Heatcube, particularly where there is strong intraday market price variation. The savings depend on location and market conditions for both natural gas and power.”
Additionally, some of Kyoto Group’s customers take advantage of incentive programmes – funding by Innovation Norway, for instance, or the European Commission, to scale up green technologies. But Bülow says the company is “absolutely market-driven” – the aim is for its products to be cost efficient without incentive programmes in a few years’ time.
California-based Antora is developing TES products that would satisfy both heat and power storage needs, with an eye on data centres. Its storage medium is “low to medium-grade graphite, very similar to what’s in your pencil,” says a spokesperson from the company. Graphite (a type of carbon) blocks, about half the size of a shipping ​container, are heated to around 2400C, which is “about a third of the ​temperature of the surface of the sun”, he explains. “They can ⁠store an incredible amount of energy, many times the energy density of a lithium-ion battery.”
The company is currently focused on products that deliver heat only, but combined heat and power solutions are “in development and close behind,” says the spokesperson. “Antora has developed thermophotovoltaic technology, or TPV, that converts the storage heat inside our system directly into electricity. In the same way that solar panels convert light from the sun (into power), we are converting the ​light from the glowing hot carbon blocks into electricity,” he explains.
While various mediums, use cases and temperatures are being explored among companies pioneering TES, there is one foundational requirement: cheap, renewable, and by ​its very nature intermittent, electricity. “Here in Spain, ⁠where I'm located right now,” says Bülow, “we have a lot of solar, so there’s very significant shifts throughout the day, which means that the price goes up and down. And that’s what we take advantage of. We charge or obtain the energy when the prices are low.”
Antora’s spokesperson also stresses the need for industrial customers to have access to varying electricity rates, which allow them to buy green electricity when it’s cheapest. “Antora and other thermal battery companies have been working with state legislators, with public utility commissions, and with utilities themselves to really show how we can enable better utilisation and greater efficiency ⁠of existing electricity systems,” ​he says.
Rosenow says it will be interesting to see how this technology takes shape as the green energy transition evolves. “What if, in the future, we have grid-scale storage, ​we have flexibility, we don’t have those big price gaps (in electricity prices) anymore? What’s the business case then?” he mused.
The answer may lie in the low capital costs of TES systems. “You invest, and within a very short time period, maybe two to three years, you actually have your money back. So it doesn't matter if, in the future, you ​don’t get the same benefit in terms of (ongoing) savings, because you’ve already paid off the entire asset.”
